clue.text: "Most everybody in the world into their graves married" (Thornton Wilder)

definitions.text: "Most everybody in the world into their graves married" (Thornton Wilder)

parts.words: "Most everybody in the world into their graves married" (Thornton Wilder)
parts.note: a line from the Stage Manager in Our Town with its verb dropped; the solver supplies the missing word of how people go into their graves

explanation.surface: A wry line from Our Town about how nearly everyone ends life as a married person.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation to complete: the printed line has lost its verb between 'world' and 'into', and the six-letter gap is filled by the word Wilder wrote.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb of the quotation describes people ascending or going up into their graves, the word Wilder used.

clue.text: … we ourselves shall be gone like ghosts at.. trevelyan

definitions.text: … we ourselves shall be gone like ghosts at.. trevelyan

parts.words: … we ourselves shall be gone like ghosts at.. trevelyan
parts.note: a line of G. M. Trevelyan's with its last word left blank after 'at'; ghosts traditionally vanish at the rooster's first call

explanation.surface: A historian's meditation that we too will vanish like spirits at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in quotation from the historian G. M. Trevelyan: ghosts in folklore flee at first light, announced by the rooster.
explanation.definitionFit: Ghosts traditionally vanish when the rooster crows at dawn, the moment that completes Trevelyan's line.

clue.text: Disregards one thousand at scene of mutiny on Sunday

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another comes before it

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
G stands for a thousand, as in a grand
the Nore, an anchorage in the Thames estuary, was where the fleet mutinied in 1797

explanation.surface: A captain shrugs off a thousand sailors rising against him on a Sunday.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nore is a sandbank anchorage at the mouth of the Thames, famous for the naval mutiny of 1797.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass over or take no notice of something is a synonym of disregarding it.

clue.text: New edition links book to Tolstoy hero

indicators.note: a new edition of a text presents it reworked, so these letters appear in a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A fresh printing of War and Peace is tied to one of its heroes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New edition' rearranges LINKS BOOK; Prince Andrei is the hero of War and Peace.
explanation.definitionFit: Prince Andrei, a central figure of War and Peace, bears this family name.

clue.text: A.J. Wentworth's was recorded by H. F. Ellis

definitions.text: A.J. Wentworth's was recorded by H. F. Ellis

parts.words: A.J. Wentworth's was recorded by H. F. Ellis
parts.note: H. F. Ellis wrote a series of books about the schoolmaster A. J. Wentworth, the last of them about his final farewell; 'recorded' hints at a song

explanation.surface: A humorist set down the final chapter of his fictional schoolmaster's career.
explanation.walkthrough: H. F. Ellis's comic schoolmaster A. J. Wentworth was given a closing book about his farewell; 'recorded' plays on a song being recorded.
explanation.definitionFit: A final performance or farewell work is called by this phrase, from the legend of a bird singing before death.

clue.text: Sean O'Casey's place of confinement

parts.note: the title of O'Casey's 1934 play set in a London park, read as a spot where someone is shut in

explanation.surface: Where the Irish playwright was kept locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: O'Casey's play takes its title from a phrase that sounds like enclosure behind park railings.
explanation.definitionFit: The play's title describes being inside an enclosure, which is a place of confinement.

clue.text: She wept in Ulster, to order

parts.note: NI is Northern Ireland, which is often called Ulster
the OBE is the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: A woman cried in Northern Ireland as she was told what to do.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth this queen wept endlessly for her slain children and was turned to a weeping stone.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical queen lost her children to Apollo and Artemis and is the classical emblem of a grieving, weeping mother.

clue.text: How Oriental shows skill at the crease

definitions.text: How Oriental shows skill at the crease

parts.words: How Oriental shows skill at the crease
parts.note: 'the crease' suggests a cricket batsman but means folds in paper, the Japanese art of folding

explanation.surface: An Asian batsman demonstrates his technique at the wicket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The crease' looks like cricket, where a batsman stands; here it is a fold in paper, as in the Japanese craft.
explanation.definitionFit: The Japanese art of folding paper into shapes is a skill exercised entirely through creases.

clue.text: Cambronne said they die but do not surrender

definitions.text: Cambronne said they die but do not surrender

parts.words: Cambronne said they die but do not surrender
parts.note: at Waterloo General Cambronne is credited with 'La Garde meurt mais ne se rend pas', about Napoleon's elite troops

explanation.surface: A French general's defiant boast at Waterloo.
explanation.walkthrough: The famous Waterloo reply attributed to Cambronne refers to Napoleon's Imperial Guard.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon's elite Imperial regiment was the Garde, the soldiers of whom Cambronne spoke.

clue.text: Dredge below arsenal location in Bleak House

indicators.note: in a down clue the second piece sits below the first in the grid

parts.note: the Royal Arsenal was at Woolwich in south-east London
a dredge is a bag net dragged along the seabed

explanation.surface: Dragging the river beneath the old munitions works.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a pointer: young Woolwich Bagnet is a character in Dickens's Bleak House, named after the place of the Royal Arsenal, a London military works.
explanation.definitionFit: The son of Mr and Mrs Bagnet in the Dickens novel bears this full name, so he is someone found within that book.

clue.text: Conveyance on which to experience Iain Banks's 1989 fantasies?

definitions.text: Conveyance on which to experience Iain Banks's 1989 fantasies?

parts.words: Conveyance on which to experience Iain Banks's 1989 fantasies?
parts.note: Banks's 1989 novel is Canal Dreams, so the vessel on which you would dream such dreams is a narrowboat on a waterway

explanation.surface: Asking what vehicle a reader needs for a Scottish novelist's dreamworld.
explanation.walkthrough: Iain Banks's 1989 novel is Canal Dreams; its 'fantasies' would be had aboard a vessel on a canal.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrow vessel for travelling waterways is the natural conveyance on which to have canal dreams.

clue.text: An English best selling novelist? The answer is a bilingual "yes"

parts.note: oui is yes in French
da is yes in Russian

explanation.surface: A quiz question about a popular English novelist, whose answer is yes in two languages.
explanation.walkthrough: The pen name of the Victorian novelist Maria Louise Ramé splits into the French and Russian words for yes.
explanation.definitionFit: Maria Louise Ramé, writing as this pen name, was a hugely popular Victorian English novelist.

clue.text: He drew attention to time spent underground by an under-age child

definitions.text: He drew attention to time spent underground by an under-age child

parts.words: He drew attention to time spent underground by an under-age child
parts.note: the first version of Alice was 'Alice's Adventures Under Ground', which its author illustrated himself

explanation.surface: Someone who publicised a child labouring down a mine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Underground' sounds like child miners; it is the original manuscript title, Alice's Adventures Under Ground, drawn by its author.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oxford don who wrote and illustrated Alice's Adventures Under Ground about a young girl wrote under this pen name.

clue.text: David, Australian novelist from over the water

explanation.surface: An Australian writer emigrating from across the sea.
explanation.definitionFit: David Ireland is an Australian novelist; across the Irish Sea from Britain lies the island of that name, so it is 'over the water'.

clue.text: Refreshing place to stop in Mario Puzo, as is well known

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the words of the author's name and the phrase after it

explanation.surface: A remark that Mario Puzo is a well-known place to pause for refreshment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points to the letters running from the end of 'Puzo' across 'as is'; 'well known' completes the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A fertile spot with water in a desert is where travellers stop to refresh themselves.

clue.text: With which to make an incisive design statement

definitions.text: With which to make an incisive design statement

parts.words: With which to make an incisive design statement
parts.note: 'incisive' is literal: the design is cut into the surface of a stone or metal

explanation.surface: A tool for a bold, sharp statement in fashion or design.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Incisive' looks like 'sharp-minded' but means cut in: a design engraved below the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: An engraved or incised figure cut into a gem or metal is a design made by cutting in.

clue.text: Lang miscellany on French town novelist

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece is placed on top of the second
a miscellany is a jumbled mixture, so the letters of the name are mixed up

parts.note: ville is French for town

explanation.surface: Andrew Lang's collected writings about a town in France, by a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lang' looks like the folklorist Andrew Lang, but it is anagram fodder signalled by 'miscellany', and 'on' stacks it above the French word; Brian Glanville is an English novelist and football writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Brian Glanville wrote fiction alongside his sports journalism, making him a writer of novels.

clue.text: Strange opera gig produces practice figuration

indicators.note: strange suggests something odd or out of order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd engagement at the opera house produces a musical flourish.
explanation.definitionFit: A broken chord played note by note is a standard figure musicians practise as an exercise.

clue.text: Hence aim revised (of heretic)

indicators.note: something revised has been altered, so these letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A heretic's aims, therefore, are amended.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' rearranges HENCE AIM; the bracketed '(of heretic)' gives the definition with 'of' as link.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of Mani's dualist religion was condemned by the early Church as a heretic.

clue.text: Mrs Radcliffe's' maid starts a new novel every two, three evenings

indicators.note: starts tells us to take the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Ann Radcliffe's servant begins a fresh book every couple of nights.
explanation.walkthrough: In Ann Radcliffe's The Mysteries of Udolpho the heroine Emily's chattering maid has this name.
explanation.definitionFit: Emily St Aubert's talkative servant in Radcliffe's Gothic novel Udolpho bears this name.

clue.text: Edith Sitwell was described by Victoria Glendinning as a high one on the move

definitions.text: Edith Sitwell was described by Victoria Glendinning as a high one on the move

parts.words: Edith Sitwell was described by Victoria Glendinning as a high one on the move
parts.note: the biographer pictured the tall, ornate poet as a walking church fixture, a 'high' one being the main one in a church

explanation.surface: A biographer's striking image of the stately poet Edith Sitwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High one' looks like a mood or a height; it is the high table of a church, which Glendinning's phrase set walking.
explanation.definitionFit: The raised table of a church is what Glendinning compared the stately, richly robed poet to.

clue.text: Some start in Italian violin works reveals devil's trill composer

definitions.text: violin works reveals devil's trill composer

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An Italian composer's violin music shows the start of his famous Devil's Trill sonata.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Some' takes part of 'start in Italian'; Giuseppe Tartini wrote the Devil's Trill sonata for violin.
explanation.definitionFit: Giuseppe Tartini was the Italian violinist who composed the Devil's Trill sonata, said to be dictated in a dream.

clue.text: "Famine sighs like — / across the field of statistics" (Derek Walcott)

definitions.text: "Famine sighs like — / across the field of statistics" (Derek Walcott)

parts.words: "Famine sighs like — / across the field of statistics" (Derek Walcott)
parts.note: a fill-in quotation from Walcott's poem; the gap is a harvesting blade whose swish is like a sigh

explanation.surface: Lines from a Caribbean poet about hunger sweeping through the numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: A quotation with a blank: Walcott likens famine to the sweep of a reaper's long curved blade.
explanation.definitionFit: A long curved blade for cutting crops sighs as it sweeps a field, and is the emblem of death and harvest.

clue.text: She is "well nourished, likely, one guesses, to become matronly later on ", said Shaw

parts.note: Shaw's stage direction describing the title heroine of his 1894 play when she first appears

clue.text: He was bound to be punished by Zeus

definitions.text: He was bound to be punished by Zeus

parts.words: He was bound to be punished by Zeus
parts.note: 'bound to be' reads as 'sure to be', but this king was literally bound to a fiery wheel by order of Zeus

explanation.surface: A man who was certain to suffer the god's wrath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to be' suggests inevitability; in myth the Lapith king was tied to a burning wheel for assaulting Hera.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lapith king who tried to seduce Hera was strapped to an eternally spinning wheel by Zeus.

clue.text: Contrary, like Hervey Allen's Anthony

explanation.definitionFit: Unfavourable or opposing means contrary; Anthony Adverse is the title hero of Hervey Allen's 1933 novel.

clue.text: All-Italian mass performance

explanation.surface: A show staged entirely by Italians.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian word for all is used in music for a passage played by the whole orchestra or chorus together.

clue.text: Jones wrote from here to it

definitions.text: Jones wrote from here to it

parts.words: Jones wrote from here to it
parts.note: James Jones's novel is From Here to ..., and the clue asks where it reaches

explanation.walkthrough: James Jones's 1951 war novel is From Here to Eternity; the clue's 'it' stands for the end of that title.

clue.text: Lawrence wrote mornings in here

explanation.surface: A novelist did his writing in the mornings at this spot.
